what: Tracks inventory, firmware, battery health, losses and operator training for thousands of drones from many vendors.
why: Drone Dominance buys from 11+ vendors and nobody manages the mixed fleet. At 200k units, logistics is the bottleneck.
wedge: One brigade's FPV fleet through a SBIR or CSO.

what: Sensor fusion and attribution software (RF, radar, acoustic, camera) for bases, data centers, stadiums, prisons and utilities.
why: $14.4B FY27 counter-UAS line plus the base-defense pilot. Commercial sites legally can only detect and report drones, so software is what they buy.
wedge: Commercial sites first, then DoD installations.

t: Synthetic data and test & evaluation for autonomy
what: Simulation and synthetic sensor data to train and certify autonomy when GPS is denied and radios are jammed.
why: New autonomy policy (the June 2026 memo, CSIS definitions) means systems need verification evidence, and the new command gets test powers.
wedge: Per-campaign service for startups going into gauntlets.

what: Maps every part to its country of origin, flags NDAA, Blue UAS and the 2027 magnet ban, and finds compliant suppliers.
why: The 1 Jan 2027 magnet ban and China's 10 Nov deadline hit hundreds of hardware vendors at once.
wedge: SaaS for drone and munitions startups. Fastest path to revenue.

t: GPS-denied navigation module ('Intel Inside' for drones)
what: A small vision, inertial and terminal-guidance board any airframe maker can integrate; later, quantum-ready.
why: Jamming is everywhere; most vendors can't build autonomy in-house. As airframes become commodities, the margin sits in components like this.

t: Contract intelligence and capture agent for small vendors
what: An LLM agent that watches SAM.gov, DIU, OTA consortia, budget documents and portfolio acquisition executives, matches openings to a product, and drafts responses.
why: Thousands of new vendors are navigating DAWG and the new acquisition rules; turning valuations into orders is the stated test.

what: Motors using ferrite or reluctance designs, or recycled magnets, for small drones and actuators.
why: China controls heavy rare earths. A compliant motor is a chokepoint product every drone maker needs.
wedge: Supply Taiwan's non-Chinese drone chain and US gauntlet vendors.

what: An autonomous interceptor under $5k for Shahed-class and FPV drones.
why: Ukraine proved the concept, and Japan, the Gulf and US bases are buying. The cost-exchange crisis is acute.
wedge: Partner with a Ukrainian team for combat data.

t: Tactical power and thermal systems for directed energy
what: Batteries, power conditioning and cooling packs that let lasers and microwave weapons fire continuously on vehicles.
why: Laser production has started (AeroVironment E-HEL) but fielding is slow (Iron Beam); power and cooling are the constraint.
wedge: Sell to laser integrators as a subsystem.

what: Licenses combat-proven Ukrainian designs (ground robots, interceptors, software) and handles compliance and US or EU production.
why: About 300 Ukrainian ground-drone firms and 500 FPV makers are looking for export routes; Brave1 is certifying exports.
wedge: Start with ground robots for logistics.

what: Low-probability-of-intercept mesh radios that keep swarms coordinated under jamming.
why: Autonomy at scale needs links that survive. Fiber works for one drone, not a swarm.
wedge: Deep tech that both Lattice and Maven ecosystems would buy.
